stem.en: A hockey puck slides across ice and gradually slows to a stop. A student says: "This proves Newton's first law is wrong — nothing was pushing it the whole time, yet it still slowed down." What's the flaw in this reasoning?

text.en: There WAS a force acting — friction from the ice — providing a small net force that decelerated the puck. The law isn't violated; it correctly predicts that a nonzero net force changes velocity.

feedback.en: Exactly the right diagnosis — the student mistook 'the ice looks smooth' for 'the ice has zero friction.' A small force is still a force.

text.en: The student is right — the first law only applies out in space, not to everyday objects on Earth.

feedback.en: The first law applies everywhere, with no exception for Earth. What's different on Earth is that friction (an unbalanced force) is almost always present — which is exactly why things here don't coast forever, not a sign the law fails.

text.en: The puck slows down because it runs out of the force the player gave it, the way a battery runs down.

feedback.en: This treats a push as a fuel supply stored inside the puck that gets 'used up' — a common but incorrect idea (physicists call it impetus theory). A push is finished the instant the stick leaves the puck; nothing about a completed push depletes afterward. What actually changes the puck's motion later is friction — a NEW force acting from outside, not the old push running down.

explanation.en: It's tempting to picture a force as something an object 'carries' after being pushed, gradually spending it until it runs out. Newton's first law replaces that picture entirely: an object's velocity only changes while a net force is currently acting on it from outside. The puck slows because ice-on-puck friction is currently acting, not because an earlier push is wearing off.

hints.en: Is 'smooth-looking ice' the same thing as 'zero-friction ice'? What force could still be acting even though you can't see it?
A force doesn't need to be dramatic to be real. Friction opposing the puck's motion is a genuine, if small, net force — and Newton's first law says exactly that a nonzero net force changes velocity.
